situations.title: The client changes requirements 2 weeks before release
situations.summary: A client asks for a change late in the project. Enter your real numbers, compare accepting, deferring and declining, then produce a Change Request you can send.

questions.label: What is the change, in one line?
questions.placeholder: Add CSV export to the reports screen

questions.label: What exactly does the client want?
questions.help: Ask the client for specifics: which screens or deliverables, what is the acceptance criterion, what happens if it is not there.

questions.label: How critical is it for the client?
questions.help: Ask: what happens to them if this is not in this release?

options.label: Must-have (blocks their launch, legal or contractual)
Important (hurts, but they can launch without it)

questions.label: Average cost per person-day (USD)
questions.help: Use the internal blended rate or your best estimate.

questions.label: Estimated effort for the change (person-days)
questions.help: Ask the team for a quick estimate. Do not guess alone.

questions.label: Schedule buffer left before the release (working days)
Share of the change cost the client will pay (%)
questions.help: 0 if the contract does not allow billing the change.

questions.label: Contract penalty per day of delay (USD, optional)
Testing and coordination overhead (%)
questions.help: Extra effort on top of the raw estimate for QA, regression, docs and meetings.
questions.why: Testing, reviews and coordination come on top of the raw estimate on almost every change.

questions.label: Share of the work that can be split across the team (%)
questions.help: Not all work can be shared. 100 means perfectly splittable.

questions.label: Productive share of a working day (%)

accept.label: Accept the change
nextSteps: Send the Change Request to the client and get written approval before any work starts.
Tell the team what is changing and re-baseline the plan together.
Update the schedule, budget and risk register.
Agree on a freeze: no further changes without a new Change Request.

defer.label: Defer to the next release
nextSteps: Offer the client a dated slot in the next release, not an open-ended promise.
Write the change into the backlog with the agreed priority.
Explain what the client gets on time instead.
Confirm with the client in writing.

decline.label: Decline the change
nextSteps: Prepare the reason in the client's terms: dates and money, not 'we are busy'.
Offer an alternative such as a smaller version or a workaround.
Raise it with your manager before the call if the client is senior.
Record the decision and the reason.

pitfalls: Saying yes in the meeting before anyone has estimated the change.
Ignoring the testing and coordination effort that comes with every change.
Absorbing the cost silently, so the client never sees what each change costs.
Telling the client about the delay after the date has already slipped.
Declining without offering a deferred or smaller alternative.

reflectionPrompts.label: What did you learn from comparing the options?
What would you do differently next time?

situations.title: Several urgent asks, not enough time
situations.summary: Two to five people want something from you this week or next. List the tasks, see which order leaves what late and who it hurts, then send your manager a clear priority proposal instead of silently working overtime.

questions.label: In one line, what is going on?
questions.placeholder: Three urgent asks landed in my first month

questions.label: Background (optional)
questions.help: Who is involved, what was promised, what you are unsure about. It goes into your proposal.

questions.label: Tasks
questions.help: Put them in the order you would do them today. That order is compared with three others.

options.label: Someone outside the organisation (client, resident, partner)
Hurts trust in me or the team

questions.label: Your working hours per week
questions.why: Your own free time sets how fast the work can go. If you enter all 40 hours, every date will be too optimistic.

questions.label: Hours per week already taken
questions.help: Meetings, support, ongoing work that will not stop
questions.why: Meetings and ongoing work do not stop because a new request arrived. We only plan with what is left.

questions.label: Hours per week I may be forgetting
questions.help: Recurring work, favours you do for others, things you promised out loud.
questions.why: Plans fail on the hours nobody wrote down. If you think about it for a minute, you can usually name some. We take these hours off your free time.

questions.label: What else might be missing?
questions.help: Verbal promises, recurring work, work you cover for others, things you depend on, holidays.

deadline.label: Earliest deadline first
nextSteps: Tell each requester the date you will deliver, today, not on the deadline.
For any task that will be late, offer a smaller version or a new date.
Ask your manager to confirm the order if a senior person's task moves.
Block the time in your calendar in this order.

stakeholder.label: Most senior requester first
nextSteps: Check that seniority really means urgency: ask what happens if it waits two days.
Tell the people whose tasks move what date they get instead.
Share the order with your manager so they can back you up.
Block the time in your calendar in this order.

impact.label: Biggest consequence first
nextSteps: Explain the order in terms of consequences: who is blocked, what it costs.
Tell the people whose tasks move what date they get instead.
Ask your manager to confirm, especially if a senior person waits.
Block the time in your calendar in this order.

custom.label: Your order (as listed)
nextSteps: Write down why this order beats the alternatives, in one sentence each.
Tell the people whose tasks will be late, before the deadline.
Ask your manager to confirm the order.
Block the time in your calendar in this order.

pitfalls: Saying yes to everyone and quietly working evenings, then missing a deadline anyway.
Letting the loudest or most senior person decide the order without asking what is really urgent.
Telling someone their task is late on the day it was due.
Not counting meetings and ongoing work, so the plan assumes 40 free hours a week.
Deciding the order alone when two requests come from people above you. That call is your manager's to make, with your data.

reflectionPrompts.label: What did seeing the orders side by side change for you?
What will you do differently the next time several asks land at once?

situations.title: Someone asks: how long will it take, and by when?
situations.summary: A manager, client or colleague wants a date from you. Give your three-point estimate and your real free hours, compare four things you could say, and send a reply that is honest about what could move the date.

questions.label: What are you being asked to do?
questions.placeholder: Quarterly churn report for the VP

questions.label: Background (optional)
questions.help: What is included, what you depend on, what is unclear. It goes into your reply.

questions.label: Best case (hours)
questions.help: Everything goes well, no surprises.
questions.why: Three estimates show how uncertain the work is. The gap between them decides how much buffer you need.

questions.label: Most likely (hours)
questions.help: What you would bet on.

questions.label: Worst realistic case (hours)
questions.help: Things go wrong in the usual ways, not a disaster.

questions.label: Free hours per week for this task
questions.help: After meetings and other work that will not stop.
questions.why: Your own free time sets how fast the work can go. If you enter all 40 hours, every date will be too optimistic.

questions.label: Lost to interruptions and context switches (%)
questions.help: Be honest: most people lose 15 to 30 %.
questions.why: People lose time to messages and switching tasks. Counting it makes the date honest.

options.label: Someone outside the organisation (client, resident, partner)

questions.label: What happens if you are late?

options.label: It hurts trust or costs something

questions.label: The date they asked for (optional)
questions.help: Leave empty if they only asked how long it takes.

questions.label: Hours per week I may be forgetting
questions.help: Recurring work, favours you do for others, things you promised out loud.
questions.why: Plans fail on the hours nobody wrote down. If you think about it for a minute, you can usually name some. We take these hours off your free time.

questions.label: What else might be missing?
questions.help: Verbal promises, recurring work, work you cover for others, things you depend on, holidays.

optimistic.label: Promise the best-case date
nextSteps: Tell them it is the best case and what must go right for it to hold.
Warn them early, the day you see it slipping.
Do not promise it in writing as a commitment.
Protect the time in your calendar from day one.

likely.label: Promise the most likely date
nextSteps: Say plainly that it is your most likely date, not a guarantee.
Name the one or two things that could move it.
Agree when you will update them if it moves.
Block the hours in your calendar now.

safe.label: Promise a safe date (with buffer)
nextSteps: Explain the date in one sentence: what it includes and the buffer you added.
If they asked for an earlier date, offer to deliver a smaller first version by then.
Do not hand over the buffer silently; tell them what it covers.
Deliver early if you can, it builds trust.

range.label: Give a range and re-check on a set day
nextSteps: Say the range and the day you will re-check, in the same message.
On the re-check day, tell them where you are, even if nothing changed.
If the range is too wide for them, ask what part could be cut or who could help.
Write the re-check date in your calendar.

pitfalls: Giving the best-case date because it is the one they want to hear.
Saying a date in the meeting before you have done a quick estimate.
Forgetting meetings, reviews and interruptions: the free hours are not 40 a week.
Telling them about the delay on the day it was due.
Giving one date with no assumptions, so nobody knows what would move it.

reflectionPrompts.label: What did the best-case, likely and safe dates show you about your estimate?
What will you do differently the next time someone asks for a date?

situations.title: I have to choose between options
situations.summary: Accept an offer, pick a tool, choose who gets the job. List what matters, score each option, and see which one wins, how safe the win is and what would change it. Then send a clear decision note.

questions.label: What do you have to decide?
questions.placeholder: Which BI tool should our team use?

questions.label: Background (optional)
questions.help: What is at stake, who else has a say. It goes into your decision note.

questions.label: Criteria
questions.help: What matters for this decision. Weight 5 is critical, 1 is nice to have. Decide the weights before you score the options.

fields.label: Weight (1-5)
fields.why: Weights say what matters most. Set them before you score the options, so the scores do not bend them.

questions.label: Options
questions.help: Score every option from 1 to 5 on each criterion above, in the same order. 5 is best for you, even for things like cost or risk.

questions.label: How hard is it to undo?
How sure are you of your scores?
questions.help: Based on facts and trials, or a gut feeling?

best.label: Go with the best weighted score
nextSteps: Check the top score against your gut. If they disagree, find out which criterion is missing.
Write down why you chose it and what would change your mind.
Tell the people it affects before they hear it from someone else.
Set a date to review the decision, and what you will look at.

safest.label: Go with the safest option
nextSteps: Check that the safest option still delivers what you need most, not only that it has no weak spot.
Write down why you chose it and what would change your mind.
Tell the people it affects before they hear it from someone else.
Set a date to review the decision, and what you will look at.

equal.label: Go with the best if all criteria weigh the same
nextSteps: Ask yourself why your weights differ from equal, and whether someone else would weigh them differently.
Write down why you chose it and what would change your mind.
Tell the people it affects before they hear it from someone else.
Set a date to review the decision, and what you will look at.

heaviest.label: Go with the best on the two heaviest criteria
nextSteps: Check what you give up on the other criteria and tell the people who care about them.
Write down why you chose it and what would change your mind.
Tell the people it affects before they hear it from someone else.
Set a date to review the decision, and what you will look at.

pitfalls: Anchoring on the first option you looked at and scoring the rest against it.
Setting the weights after you have seen the scores, so they confirm what you already wanted.
Scoring what you know best instead of what matters most.
Treating a 3-point lead as certain when the scores are guesses.
Deciding alone when other people carry the consequences.

reflectionPrompts.label: What did the scores and the flip points show you that you had not seen?
What will you do differently the next time you have to choose between options?
